title: Rivet SDK: first-10-requests experiments & quick templates (draft)
content:
Overview:
This is an experimental sketch for a super-lightweight developer onboarding flow aimed at optimizing the critical first 10 requests a new SDK user makes. Goal: make the first 10 successful interactions so frictionless that devs hit a meaningful demo within 15 minutes. Draft is intentionally rough — playbook + sample commands + checkpoints + telemetry contract ideas.

Why "first 10"?
- Observational hypothesis: most drop-off happens before the app issues ~10 meaningful calls (auth, env, client init, first generation/embedding, error handling).
- If we make those 10 interactions predictable and resilient, downstream retention and conversion improves.

Success metrics (experiments to run):
- 1) Time-to-first-successful-response (TTFSR): median under 5 minutes for a clean environment.
- 2) First-10 completion rate: percent of new signups that complete 10 non-empty requests within first session. Target: +20% vs baseline.
- 3) Error surface: top 5 uncaught failure modes observed during initial requests.

Quick heuristics for the flow (dev UX):
- Step 0: One-line install (pip/npm) + minimal README header
- Step 1: Obtain API key -> sample env var export or OS keyring guidance
- Step 2: Minimal client init with explicit region example (hosted/dedicated hints)
- Step 3: First call: model-info / ping / health check (fast, deterministic)
- Step 4: Demo call 1: short text generation (streaming optional)
- Step 5: Demo call 2: embeddings example (small vector)
- Step 6: Error handling example (timeout/circuit) + retry best practice
- Step 7: Telemetry: show how SDK emits event for request_count, latency_ms, model_selected
- Step 8: Local dev/CI smoke: a one-file sample app that runs all above in <10s tests

Minimal README template (to be auto-generated):
- Title + 1-line elevator
- Install
- Quickstart (3–6 lines) -> exports API_KEY; run example.py
- Troubleshooting (env var tips, common error codes)
- Links (console, pricing, security)

Concrete command samples (shell-first path):
- pip install rivet-sdk
- export REDWOOD_API_KEY=sk-...
- python -c "from rivet import Client; c=Client(); print(c.ping())"
- python examples/quick_gen.py --model=gpt-lite --prompt="Summarize this in one sentence."

Edge-case smoke tests to include in the starter package:
- Missing API key -> deterministic helpful error (code: 401-SDK-CLI) + link to console
- Rate-limited -> backoff example + SDK-provided RetryPolicy usage snippet
- Unsupported model endpoint -> human-friendly message + fallback to compatible model list
- Local network down -> offline hint + guidance for retry windows

Telemetry contract (initial proposal):
- Required events: request.start, request.end, request.error
- Attributes (per event): api_key_hash (sha256 prefix), model_name, region, route (generation|embedding|ping), latency_ms_bucket, response_tokens_estimate, status_code_category
- Usage: events emitted to default logger and optionally to customer telemetry hooks. Keep payload small.

Sample one-file smoke app (high-level):
- init client from env
- ping -> if fails, print actionable fix
- generate with model selection hint
- embed a short string
- print telemetry summary (counts + mean latency) local-only console output

Developer-facing templates to land in repo:
- examples/quick_gen.py (script + comments)
- examples/ci_smoke.sh (runs headless in CI, exits 0 if all good)
- examples/README-first10.md (narrative walkthrough)

Instrumentation & telemetry capture in CI:
- CI runs the quick smoke with a sandbox key (quota-limited) on every merge to main for the SDK repo branch experiment/first-requests
- Collect TTFSR metric and small histogram for latency. Upload artifact to experimental dashboard (Rivet onboarding board).

Observability hooks for product folks:
- Simple dashboard: funnel (new signups -> install -> first ping -> first generation -> 10 requests)
- Error breakdown: auth, region mismatch, timeout, rate-limit, validation error
- Heatmap: which sample models used by devs in first session (helps surface default model choice tuning)

Troubleshooting playbook (for support/SRE):
- If dev reports failure at ping: check API key validity, region mismatch, blocked IP list in firewall for private deployments
- If generation fails intermittently: check model variant fallbacks, quota exhaustion, recent rollout changes (canary flag history)
- If CI smoke fails after merge: is the sandbox key rotated? check credential store secrets rotation log

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Default model selection: do we bias toward cheapest-fastest or slightly larger model with better responses for first-run wow? (possible A/B test)
- Should SDK auto-fallback across regions or require explicit region param? (safety + latency tradeoffs)
- Telemetry opt-in defaults: do we enable minimal anonymous telemetry by default or require opt-in at install time? (privacy/legal)
- Do we ship the quick CI smoke in main repo or as a GitHub action template repository for easier reuse?

Next steps (short list):
- [ ] Sync with product-hosted-api on recommended default model and sandbox key policy (owner: Arjun)
- [ ] Prototype quick_gen.py and ci_smoke.sh, commit to github branch (owner: Maya)
- [ ] Create dashboard placeholders and wire TTFSR metric from CI runs (owner: Lena)
- [ ] Draft minimal telemetry sampling policy and privacy blurb for README (owner: Diego)

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep the sample code intentionally naive. The goal is cognitive relief, not a production pattern.
- Avoid heavy abstractions in quickstart; show advanced helpers later in docs.
- Consider a tiny web-based sandbox (one-click run) later but defer until we validate local-first path increases conversion.

References and links:
- jira/RIVET-87 (experiment tracking)
- github.com/redwood-inference/rivet-sdk (prototype branch)
- internal slack: #rivet-onboarding (thread pinned with early feedback)

End of draft. This doc can be split into: (A) README template + examples (B) support runbook (C) telemetry contract + dashboard wires. Keep iteration tight — ship minimal first, measure, iterate.
